claim: SFO's Quiet Airport program removed approximately 90 minutes of daily announcement time throughout the terminal and reduced announcements at gate seating areas by roughly 40%.
source_title: Inside San Francisco Airport's 'Quiet Airport' Initiative
supporting_excerpt: The program resulted in a 40% reduction of announcements at gate seating areas and 90 minutes of reduction in the whole terminal each day.
denominator: SFO daily terminal announcement total (baseline undisclosed)
caveat: Secondary reporting; SFO primary methodology and baseline measurement not verified. Airport Context Packet §9 flags that the underlying methodology is unverified.

claim: SFO's methodology zoned public-address delivery so that A-gate announcements no longer bleed into B-gate seating, retaining only final-call cross-zone broadcasts.
source_title: San Francisco Airport Removed 90 Minutes of Daily Noise — Travelers Say It Changed Everything
supporting_excerpt: The SFO Customer Care team realigned where public announcements would be made to page passengers only in necessary areas of the airport. For example, if you're at an A gate, you're not going to be hearing announcements from the B gates with the exception of final calls.
caveat: Secondary reporting summarizing SFO Customer Care policy; primary SFO policy document not obtained for this brief.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175 recommends a minimum Speech Transmission Index of 0.45 and a signal-to-noise ratio of 10-15 dB for public-address broadcasts in pier-style airport departure lounges.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems
page_or_section: Chapter 3 — Speech Intelligibility; Chapter 4 — Physical Factors Affecting PA Intelligibility
supporting_excerpt: A good target for announcement levels is a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 10 to 15 dB… codes and application standards typically recommend a minimum STI of 0.45 or 0.50.
caveat: STI thresholds are design-level recommendations; local codes may impose stricter requirements. Verified against the National Academies Press open-access chapter view.

claim: In ACRP 175's industry survey, 69% of respondents rated high reverberation as one of the most important factors hindering passengers' ability to understand PA announcements.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems
page_or_section: Chapter 4 — Physical Factors Affecting PA Intelligibility
supporting_excerpt: 69% of industry survey respondents judged high reverberation to be one of the most important factors hindering passengers' ability to understand PA announcements.
denominator: ACRP 175 survey respondent pool (n not stated in this excerpt)
caveat: Respondent count not captured in this excerpt; readers should consult the report's methodology chapter for sample size.

claim: The Joint Commission established clinical alarm system safety as a National Patient Safety Goal (NPSG.06.01.01) effective January 1, 2014, with a two-phase implementation requiring hospitals to first prioritize alarm safety and then establish policies to reduce alarm-related risks by January 1, 2016.
source_title: The Joint Commission Announces 2014 National Patient Safety Goal
supporting_excerpt: The Joint Commission implemented the alarm NPSG in two phases, with the first phase set to go into effect January 1, 2014… and the second phase beginning January 1, 2016, introducing requirements to mitigate those risks.
caveat: Cross-domain analogy for airport announcement governance; NPSG applies to accredited hospitals, not airports.

claim: A Johns Hopkins ICU study observed an average of 771 clinical alarms per bed per day over a 12-day period, illustrating the scale of alarm exposure that drove the Joint Commission's action on alarm fatigue.
supporting_excerpt: A Johns Hopkins study found that over a 12-day period, one ICU had an average of 771 alarms per bed per day.
data_vintage: Johns Hopkins study period undated in excerpt
caveat: Secondary reporting; primary Johns Hopkins study citation not resolved in this brief. Used as illustrative magnitude, not as universal ICU baseline.

claim: The Washington Dulles Main Terminal, designed by Eero Saarinen and opened in 1962, received the AIA Twenty-Five Year Award and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.
supporting_excerpt: Airport Context Packet §5 confirms 1978 National Register listing and 1966 AIA Honor Award; Wikipedia entry corroborates Saarinen authorship and 1962 opening.
airport_or_entity: Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) — Main Terminal
caveat: Wikipedia used as convenience citation for building history; historic-register status is corroborated in the run's Airport Context Packet.

claim: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual issued by the Office of Engineering, described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on airport property, and it is the standing vehicle by which MWAA binds consultants, contractors, and tenants to design requirements.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), Section 7
page_or_section: Section 7 — MWAA Design Manual and standards apparatus
supporting_excerpt: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual, plus Specifications and Estimating and Scheduling Standards, issued by the MWAA Office of Engineering. The Design Manual is described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property, updated annually.
caveat: Context packet is the assembled Stage-0 record; underlying primary Design Manual document was not independently retrieved for this brief.

claim: A new 15-year MWAA Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, carrying approximately a $9 billion initial capital construction program split roughly $6.99 billion at IAD and $2.39 billion at DCA.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), Section 4
supporting_excerpt: A new 15-year Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, replacing the prior agreement. At execution the agreement carried an approximately $9 billion capital construction program.
caveat: MII thresholds and cost-recovery categorization are not established in the context packet and must not be inferred from convention. Used in this brief to argue that tenant-audio requirements must bind through the AULA in addition to the Design Manual.

claim: The January 29, 2025 midair collision at DCA between PSA/American 5342 and a U.S. Army UH-60L killed 67 people; the February 2026 NTSB final report attributed multiple failures across FAA, air traffic control, and military operations, including FAA placement of a helicopter route too close to a runway approach.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), Section 8
supporting_excerpt: January 29, 2025 midair collision at DCA (PSA/American 5342 and a U.S. Army UH-60L) killed 67 people. The February 2026 NTSB final report found multiple failures across FAA, air traffic control, and military operations.
caveat: Used in this brief as context for board-level risk tolerance around any 'reduce announcements' framing; not as a technical acoustics finding.

claim: Occupational noise exposure of employees is regulated by OSHA under 29 CFR 1910.95, which imposes hearing-conservation program obligations on employers when time-weighted average exposure reaches or exceeds 85 dB(A) over eight hours.
supporting_excerpt: The employer shall administer a continuing, effective hearing conservation program… whenever employee noise exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average sound level (TWA) of 85 decibels measured on the A scale (slow response).
airport_or_entity: US OSHA (applies to airport employers as covered employers)
caveat: Cited to support the brief's tangent that a quiet-by-design standard has an occupational-health defense in addition to a passenger-experience one; MWAA-specific dosimetry not obtained.
